blocks.x: This is Bill Russell interviewing Mr. Dollier up at 732 St. Peter Street. And the date is, I have to look it up, what is the date? It's May the 22nd, I believe. May 22nd, 1965. Your name is spelled D-O-L-L-I-O-L-E. I have your card here and it's pronounced Dollier, is that right?
That's right, Dollier.
Dollier, Dollier.
Milford Dollier.

The first name is Milford? Milford, yeah. Milford. Can you tell me just when you were born, if you don't mind? On the 23rd day of October, 1903. 1903. And was that right in New Orleans here? New Orleans, Louisiana, 2010 Bourbon Street. Downtown. Downtown, yeah. Is that where, is it crossover on Rampart Street on the other side?
On the other side of Rampart, there's three squares.
Up in there.
Going to the woods.
Yeah. Uh-huh. Can you tell me, did your folks play any music, your father and mother?
My daddy played trumpet years ago.
Your daddy?
Uh-huh, Joseph Dollier.
Joseph. Uh-huh. You mentioned a minute ago you had a brother too that played trumpet. Yeah, he played trumpet.
Joseph Dollier Jr.
Was he older or younger? He's older, one year older. One year older. Uh-huh. Did your mother play anything? No, my mom never played nothing.
She used to sing little songs and things around the house on white days and things, you know.
Yes. Can you tell me when you first heard music, when you got interested in music and what?

Oh, I used to follow the bands when they played the fumes and different things and I got interested in the drums. And I used to like to hear this fellow, Bebe, used to play drums for the, I forgot what band it was, Manny Perez band.
Is that Bebe Matthews?
Bebe Matthews from over the river.
Yes.
And I used to like to see him, I used to follow him all the time.
Did he play snare drum or? Snare drum. Uh-huh. That was with Manuel Perez. Right. Is that what they called the Onward Band or do you remember?
Yeah, I think it was. I was quite small. You know.
Is that over in your neighborhood, those Perez?
Yeah, all around used to come to the church, right around the corner from my home.
What church was that?
That was Morris Brown Church on Zurich Street.
What kind of a church? It was a Baptist church. Baptist church, yeah. Did you all belong to that church? No, I was Catholic. You were Catholic.
I was born as Catholic.
Yeah. Can you tell me about your very first instrument, what you started on? Was it drums or what?
Drums. I used to play on the steps and different things like that until I bought a drum. And then after I bought a snare drum. I, uh...
About how old were you when you started beating on the steps even?
Oh, I was a kid around about 15.
Mm-hmm.
15-year-old.
Yeah. And how old were you when you got your first drums?
Well, about 19 years. I was about 19 years.
19. Yeah. Now, did you have a teacher?
Well, I started with Louis Contrell, Mr. Contrell, the old drummer.
Yeah. I never knew him, but I know his son, of course.
Yeah. My daddy recommended to him, you know.
Yeah.
And I took a few lessons with him and then, I don't know, I just stopped and I liked the jazz. I didn't care too much about reading. I'm sorry I didn't keep it up then.
Yeah. Well, a lot of good drummers never did bother with the reading anyway, of course.
But he was very interested, man. I should have kept...
Was he a pretty strict teacher? Yeah, he was pretty strict.
You couldn't put nothing in it. You couldn't put nothing over.
You know who he was playing with in those days or what band he was in?
He was playing with Manny Perez on the roof garden.
The roof garden.
Yeah.
Up there where the city hall is now. Deeply Temple. Yeah, right there.
That's years ago. Yes.
Did you have a full set of drums when you started? I did. You got bass drum and snare. Yeah, bass drum and everything.
Snairs, cowbells, cymbals and everything.
How many cowbells did you use in those days? Four.
Yeah.
Albert Giles had a set of four of them. Yeah, he did. I remember Baby Dodds had a set of four in Chicago. I always saw his. Yeah. And what kind of cymbals did you use?
I had one large crash cymbal and then I had a... Was that the Chinese one?
Yeah. That turned up on the edges and all that? Right, yeah. That's it.
Made in the Chinese style. Yeah. Mm-hmm.
And then another, was it a Turkish cymbal, regular? Yeah, I had a Turkish cymbal.
Yeah.
That's true. When you started, did you have one of those cymbals down on the drum that the pedal would get there? Yeah, we did.
It was an overhead beater we had first. Yeah. You had the overhead beater. Yeah.
And then after, then the flow beater come in style. Yeah. And I used both.
I worked on both of them.
Yeah. You hadn't had one of those old overhead beaters anymore? No.
I wish I could get one.
That thing is... Yeah. That's right, yeah. You don't know anybody that has one around, I guess.
No, I wish I would.
I guess everybody threw them out when they bought their good pedals. It would be nice to have one now to see how they work.
Uh-huh.
Can you tell me about the first job you ever played now? Yeah, the first job I played was with Euless Jean.
He was a trumpet player, a good friend of mine. Yes, I heard him play one time. Yeah, he's the cause I start playing drums, because he played the trumpet and I said, well, I'll play the drums.
Do you know anything about him? I'm not sure if he's still living. Somebody said...
Yeah, he's living. He's living. Him and I worked together over the river on a project. He's blaspheming, you know.
How long have you, since you've seen him?
It was, uh, no, it must be about four months since I said...

Well, that late then. Yeah. Because somebody told me that once he went up like Baton Rouge or someplace... Yeah, he's living in Baton Rouge, but he come here to work. But he comes here to work. Well, I didn't know.
Uh-huh.

Yeah. I saw him about 1944. It's the only time I ever saw him and heard him play. You did, eh? Uh-huh. That's been, oh, years ago now. Oh, yeah. Twenty-one years ago. Yeah. Let's see if there's anything else about your drum set while I can think of it. Uh-huh. Did you use that tom-toms?
Yeah, I used a little tom-tom. Uh-huh.

What kind was that like? The Chinese... A little, uh, Chinese tom-tom. Chinese tom-tom. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Also, uh, woodblock. Did you mention if you had any woodblock? Yeah. I played a woodblock too. Is there anything else you can tell us about, uh, Cartrell, Louis Cartrell, how he played or what style? Oh, I know he was a very good drummer.

I can tell you he was a very good drummer. And I was interested in what he showed me, you know, what he taught me. And he's a very nice fella to get along with, cause nice disposition, you know. When I'd go to his house, he would greet me with a smile. Yeah.
Where did he live about then?
He lived down in it between, uh, Durbin and Roomba. Uh-huh. That's why he was here.
And you went to his house then for lessons? I went to his house, yeah.
Twice a week.
When you went there, did you take your drums with Durbin? He had a pad. He had a pad. We're gonna pad.
I just had to take the sticks, the little pad made out of skins, stuffed with cotton or something like that.
Do you remember anything, I know it's hard to remember all the way back when you started, but what kind of sticks did he advise you to have? Heavy sticks or light sticks or anything?
No, this was light, it was A1 I think it was. A1. Uh-huh. It was A1 I think.
Yeah.
I can't remember that good.
So you worked mostly just on the drum pad then, the snare sticks. Yeah, when he was teaching me. How often did you go for lessons, about once a week? Twice a week a week. Twice a week.
It was just 50 cents a lesson.
About how long were the lessons?
About a half hour, four or five minutes.
He was interested in teaching.
Yeah. Because my dad was good friends with him, you know.
If that bird bothers you, we can put him in the other room.
Oh yeah. That's okay.
He must like it, he's on your shoulder. Can you tell me anything about the brass bands, if you ever heard Louis Contrall and the brass bands?
Well yeah, I've heard them with Paris.
Paris. Which did he play, bass drum or snare drum? He played snare drum. Snare drum.
Yeah.

Now to get back to your first job, which we sort of interrupted, you mentioned it was with Euless Jean. Do you know anything about him, where he came from? Was he from New Orleans itself or from the country?
Yeah, he was born in New Orleans and he was raised, we was raised, he was raised on Ayquart Street and I was raised on Bourbon Street.
Is he about your same age?
He's the same age as me. He was born in December.
In December.
And I'm born in October. Yeah.

Yeah, we're the same age. Same age. You know, if he took lessons from anybody? Yeah, he took lessons from his uncle, Nelson Jean. Oh, yeah, I never knew anything about him. I never did talk to Euless Jean either. No. And he may get down here though sometime, I guess you say he comes down here to work anyway. Yeah, if I ever see him, I'll have him to come see him. If he's ever here at night, tell him to come by the hall here. I sure will. A lot of people will be glad to see him, I know.
Yeah, I'm going to pass the word around to his brother when I see him.
A lot of people have heard of him, but does he play trumpet anymore?
No, I don't think. I don't know if he's interested in it or what, you know. Yeah.
But I'll talk to him about it. I just heard him play one night at a lawn party about 1944. Yeah. Who else was in the band, that first job you had?
Oh, I just can't remember that. It was a four-piece band. That's four pieces.
I just can't remember. They used clarinet or trombone?
It was a clarinet player, but I lost trace of him, who he was. I just can't remember him.

I was interested in that picture that you loaned to Al Rose, which he wants to have in a book. I have those pictures of Al Rose here now. I've been going over those pictures. I might be able to find it, but can you remember now who else was in that band, that picture? Tuxedo band? Yes, in the tuxedo. Oh, yeah.
I could name most all of them. It was Eddie Mariah, Joan Mariah, Lawrence Mariah.
John played banjo, did he? Right.
Bush Hall. Oh, yes. Doug O'Neill. Abby Foster. A Chinese, that one. A Chinese, yeah. A Chinese. A Chinese, yeah. A Chinese. A Chinese. A Chinese, yeah.
A Chinese.
A Chinese. A Chinese. A Chinese. A Chinese. A Chinese. A Chinese. A Chinese. A Chinese. A Chinese.
A Chinese. A Chinese. A Chinese. A Chinese. A Chinese.
A Chinese. A Chinese. A Chinese. A Chinese. A Chinese.

I might be able to find that picture in the other room in a few minutes and we can go over that. What was your other bands that you played with? You mentioned the Utilis Gene was your first band. Oh, I played, yeah, and I played in my oldest. About how old were you when you first played? About 19. 19 when you played with them. That was just a four piece. Where did they play? Any special places?
No, just around town, different little house parties, you know. This was for some Italian people we played that night. I always think about my first job.
Yeah, something you usually never forget.
About my brother, we had an orchestra. I played with him for quite a while. It was the original cloverleaf. I played with them.
They call that the original cloverleaf. That was the brother that was the trumpeteer. The trumpeteer. Is he still living? Yeah, he's living. But doesn't play?
He doesn't play anymore. He's sick, you know. I don't think he can be. He tries, but I think he... I don't think he can come up to the stand.
Unless you keep at it all the time, it's hard to keep your lip in shape and all.
Yeah.
Can you remember any other bands now that you played with? Sorry, you mentioned your brother's band and Euless Jean, some of the very earliest ones.
Well, I played in rake up bands like I played with Buddy Petit. I played with Chris Kelly. I played with Celestine too.
How long were you with Chris Kelly? Do you remember who else was in the band? No, well, I just played at Giles when he hired me like that, you know, when he was drumming.
But I never was in the regular. My regular was with Cloverleaf and when Saeed was taken sick, I played in his place almost a year. Probably in the Young Tuxedo band. In the Young Tuxedo?
Yeah, huh. That's the one that the picture was taken. Yeah, uh-huh.
There were so many different fellas I played with. Oh, Raymond Brown.

Do you remember anything about Raymond Brown's band? It was Twat just told us a few minutes ago that he played his first job with Raymond Brown. Yeah. And he was a trombonist, I know. I think he was some relative of H.E. Miners, wasn't he? I think once had a picture that H.E. loaned us. Well, I know. Do you remember anything about him? Because he's dead now, I understand. Yeah, I understand, yeah.

And his brother was a trumpet player, Bat. Bat Brown. We used to call him Bat Brown. And we used to go to rehearsal way uptown. And he used to come down here all the time. He was, this fella was well known. He had plenty of little jobs. He played plenty of jobs with him. How did he play? What type of trombone was his name? He was a good trombone player. Like anybody else that you can think of playing today that we might- Oh, he played all the style of his gym down there.
Something like Jim Robinson. Yeah, he played all that style. He was a good man. A pretty loud tone and all. Yeah, yeah. Very loud. Very loud. You know when he died or how long- No, I didn't know.
When I heard of it, you know, he had been dead.
He was a good trombone player.
Good trombone player.
Good trombone player. Like anybody else that you can think of that playing today that we might-
Oh, he played all the style of his gym down there. Something like Jim Robinson. Yeah, he played all that style. He's a good man. Yeah, pretty loud tone and all.
Yeah, yeah. Very loud. Very loud. Very loud. You know when he died or how long-
No, I didn't know. He had been dead several years.
I never did know him.
Because I got out the music business. I was so interested in traveling and plastering business.
That's why I lost a year I'm a plasterer. I guess you knew Johnny St. Cyr, did you? Good friend of mine.
I played music with him with Georgie Parker Band at Happyland and out the lake. We played there about four years.
When was that? That wouldn't be awfully long ago I guess. With Georgie Parker?
Well, that was in the late 40's.
Yeah, 1940's.
Then Mealy Bones I played by the Harmony Inn. Oh yes.
I might have even heard you down there. I heard that band. Maybe you were in there one time.
I didn't even know you. But this guy played the piano. He died too. I just remember his name now.

Walter. Walter. Walter Decoe. Oh, is he dead? I didn't know for sure if he's dead. Yeah, he's dead. I knew he wasn't playing anymore. They told me he was dead. That's what I heard. Yeah, I've never heard for sure if he died. Lawrence Torkum. Yeah. I knew him.
Emile Bones. I worked down there quite a while. At the Harmony Inn.
Yeah.
Three nights a week I played. Was that in the 1940's?
Yeah, that was in the 40's. When did you quit the music business? You really haven't quit yet I guess. You still have your drums? No, I'm coming back on the chair.

I have a set of drums and everything. I have a good set of drums. And, well I slacked down say around 1949 I think. Or 1950. Yeah, around 1950. It ain't too far back. No, no. You don't lose too much practice.
No, no. You learn something that you really know you never forget like that. No, no, you never forget.
You'll be a little rusty but you come back strong. Yeah.
Yeah. Did you ever play much parade work on the streets?
No, I never played much parade in the streets. No. All my job was sit-in jobs.
Yeah. Who were your favorite drummers when you were young? Of course I know you must have liked Cottrell or you wouldn't have taken lessons.

Yeah, I liked him and Chani and I were good friends. And I learned a whole lot from him and he was interested in me and another fellow I was interested in playing, I used to like, he was playing with Alfred Williams. Oh yes, yes.
He just died a year or two ago now. Good drummer. Yeah.
And I was interested around him so the fellas got out and learned different things, you know.
Yeah, Alfred is left handed, I guess you're right handed, are you? Yeah, right hand drummer.
Thank you.
Uh huh. And uh... Joe Watkins is left handed too. There are two here. Uh huh. And most left handed drummers are good drummers. Can you remember any other left handed drummers around?

Uh huh. You know, uh, yeah I know, Clay Bair, uh, he's about to play trumpet there. He played with, uh, his name is Orny. I can't think now. He played with, uh, George Lewis. Little short bright fella.
Yeah, I can't think. Because I knew another...

George Lewis, something like that. I knew another left hand drummer in Chicago, Snaggs Jones. He left here very early though. Played with King Oliver, now way back. He was left handed. Um, we were talking about some of your favorite drummers. Do you remember any others on parade that you used to like?
Do you remember any others on parade that you used to like? Especially?
If you'd follow on parade that you used to like?
Especially? Yeah, but most likely.
I didn't know.

I knew another left hand drummer in Chicago, Snaggs Jones. He left here very early though. Uh huh. Played with King Oliver, now way back. Oh yeah. He was left handed. Um, we were talking about some of your favorite drummers. Do you remember any others on parade that you used to like? Especially? If you'd follow on a parade?

Yeah, but most likely, under these fellas used to play, the parades could look like their band had the job, contract with the societies. That was the time, yeah. And most likely all the time it would be Charney would be with the Tuxedo band, and Alfred Williams, and Contra was with parades for last month. And the Bay was with the Hornwood band. Oh yeah. And all that sort of thing. I could remember that.
Do you remember the other Matthews brothers that played?

Yeah, I remember Bill when he played drums. He was a good drummer too. I heard he won the parade too. In late years he played one parade once. Yeah, he was a good drummer. Yeah. He was a good drummer. He was a good drummer.
Yeah. He was a good drummer. Yeah. He was a good drummer. Yeah. Yeah.
I know him too. Yeah.
Which one do you think was the best drummer?
I think that Bebe was the best drummer.
The best drummer in the family. I think, yeah.
Because I heard him play in the string band and everything like that, you know.
In the parades what did Bebe play? A snare drum? A snare drum.
A snare drum.
A snare drum. It was a good snare drum. You mentioned like a string band now. Does that mean with the trumpet and trombone and all too? Yeah.
We used to call it string band because they'd have the guitar and the bass.
But it didn't mean just the guitar and bass and mandolin or violin or something. It meant the full dance band. Uh-huh.
And we would call the brass band, you know, the nine pieces or the twelve pieces like that on the streets. Yeah.
That was the brass band. Yeah. And the string band meant a regular dance orchestra. That's right.
That's right.
How far back did they use that term, string band?
Oh, they used it during my time. I heard it, you know, string band. But they didn't use it awfully, too often.
They don't use that now anymore. No, they don't use that anymore. Like they wouldn't call Sweet Emmas a string band. I know. First they had string bass but no guitars. Uh-huh.
But they died out. You know, people never used it too much. I heard the elder people used it.
That's what I know it was used a long time ago. Now I'm sort of surprised when I hear people talking about a string band.
Oh, yeah.

Because years ago I thought they meant like a string trio. Yeah, I know what you mean. With guitar, bass, mandolin, or violins, yeah. Something without any horns. Right. But the string band meant with the horns and all then, too. And drums and all, too, in the string band. Yeah.
Uh-huh.
Yeah, it's interesting that they used that term. Uh-huh. Any other favorite drummers that you had that you can think of that were good in those days?
Oh, yeah. Happy and Zuda Singleton. You remember Ziddy then?
Oh, yeah.
I knew him in New York. Oh, yeah. I remember them all, yeah. I remember when he played at the Lyrics Theater. Oh, yeah.
Is that Robichaux's band? Yeah, uh-huh.
Yeah, Robichaux. But Happy was pretty good. Which Happy was that?
Red Happy or Black Happy? Red Happy. Red Happy, yeah.
Uh-huh. He was very good.
Where did you hear him?
Oh, he used to be, he played with Chris Kelly while, and then he was a show drummer. He used to play in the show all the time, at the Lyrics Theater.
At the Lyrics. I mean Robichaux's band. Yeah. Was that before Zuddy or after Zuddy? That was before Zuddy. Before Zuddy.
Yeah. And then Joe Lindsey, I remember him, he was a good drummer.
Oh, yeah. I met him in Chicago. I never did hear him play, though. Yeah, he was a good drummer, yes. He was a friend of the-
Little good.
Oh, boy, that's your car. I noticed here on your car, you say you do plastering, and you used to, did you ever work with Johnny St. Cyr on the same jobs?
Oh, yeah. Him and I worked on the same jobs together.

We plastered together and we played music together. Yeah. Uh-huh. Because I last saw him in California and he was doing plastering then. I spoke to him in California last year. Oh, you were out there. Yeah, on Wall Street.
He lived out there. Oh, yeah.
He still out. I stayed at his house, Professor Minetta and I, about a month. Yeah, we stayed there.
Well, I lived there's about six squares from him. Oh, really? But I never could get to see him. And I left before I saw him, but I really wanted to see him because-
He's awfully busy, I guess. He was a good friend of mine.
Yeah, he used to go to work at one o'clock. Yeah. And that's the time I'd be waking, you see.

Now, since he works out of Disneyland, it's way out. They have to go there early, I guess. Uh-huh. Have you always lived downtown in about this same section? Same section. That's our bond there. Yeah.
And I live this- I born there 2010 and I live at 2028. That's about four houses.

Let's see, Bourbon Street is- what do they call that now? Is that- Oh, it's the same street then? Yeah, yeah. The same street you were born on, right? Right, yeah. I forgot. I know they changed the name and I wasn't sure what they called it.
You know, I tell fellas, I say, I'm born on Bourbon Street, so some fellas would say, oh, he's just saying that Bourbon Street is famous.
Yeah, because all the clubs are-
But during that time, yeah, during that time it was Bourbon Street all the way to the lake.
Yeah, it's curved around, I know. Uh-huh.
And it is continued at Caleret and called it Poggle. And that's around 1936 somewhere around. They changed that then.

Somewhere around that time. I know Lizzie Miles used to tell people she was born on Bourbon Street like between Burgundy and Dolphin or something. Right. People wouldn't believe her. They'd say, well, that doesn't cross those streets, it goes the same direction. Right. They wouldn't believe her. They wouldn't believe it. That's right. They'd say that they changed the name. Uh-huh. And it turns down. Now let's see, any other drummers on parade, I started to ask, did you ever remember Ernest Trepanier?
Yeah, yeah, exactly, yeah. He was supposed to be a good bass drummer, they tell me.
He was a good bass drummer, he was. Did you hear him in dances too or just on the parade?
Yeah, I heard him in several band dances. He plays pretty good. He was a pretty good drummer. Yeah.
Of course, Louis Armstrong always talks about Black Benny, the drummer uptown around Perdido Street and all that played. Yeah, I remember him too. You got to hear him. I remember him.
Yeah, I remember him.
Of course. You were talking about some of the bands you played with. Do you remember when you played with Buddy Petit, anybody else in the band?
Yeah, it was Lawrence Mariah, Eddie Mariah and.
Did Eddie play bass those days then?
Yeah, Eddie played bass and Lawrence played the banjo. Yeah. Let's see.
And was there anybody else in Chris Kelly's band? I started to ask you a minute ago if you remembered anybody else who played clarinet or? Mealy Barnes played clarinet. Mealy Barnes.
Yeah. Uh huh.
Can you remember a few of the places you played, even if they were only for a night or two sometimes, some of the old halls, you know?
Well, I played at the Economy Hall, I played at the Poiseuilers Hall, at the New Hall, at the Hopes Hall.
Yeah. They tore that down at last. Yeah, they tore it down because of the storm damage. After the hurricane last September. Mm-hmm.
And I played at the merry-go-round once. It was way up in town.
Oh, it's still up there, I guess. Yeah. They still have parades, way up there. Yeah. I played at the Tulane Club. Yeah, that's still there, I guess. Yeah. Uh huh. Gravier, I believe.
Well, them is all noted halls for dances and banquets and weddings and things.
What nights did they usually have the banquets and dances and all of those halls?
Well, the banquets used to be on Mondays. That would be from 1 to 6.
In the afternoon, the early evening. Yeah, right.
And the other dances would be from 8 to 3 in the morning.
Yeah. Yeah. What nights did they usually have the dances? Sunday nights. Sunday.
Yeah, particularly on Sundays.
Is there any reason for having it on a Sunday night?
No, it looked like it. I don't know.
Because usually Saturday night nowadays, you know, is the big night everybody goes out.
Yeah, it was a big night, but during them time it was, I don't know, a regular tradition of giving a dance on a Sunday night.
On a Sunday night.
Very Sunday. Then they started on Monday nights, giving dances. Yeah. Excuse me.
I'm sorry. Are they banquets any certain day for those? Mondays. Mondays.
Mondays was the banquet days from 1 to 6. What did they call it?

Society's a banquet day. What's the Creole name they call it? The banquet. Blanquet. Blanquet. Yeah. Okay. And were those mostly for the club members or did they sell tickets to those? No, it was an invitation.

It was a society. At the end of the year they'd take money out to treasure and they would have a big layout of ham and beer and soft drinks and chicken and tater salad and all that kind of stuff. Everybody would join and be happy.
I remember the Musicians Union, I went to a few of those every year. Those were up at San Jacinto Hall. Yeah.
Well I played at San Jacinto Hall too.
They'd always have a big feed there once a year. Yeah. Do you know anything about the union in the real old days? Did they have a union or was it very strong?

Well they did have a union and Celestine was the president. And they always kept a card but it just got out of my way. And how it got out I don't know. It was just like that picture I had. That picture I had was 40-something years. Yeah. And I kept up with the picture. And I always told my wife, don't destroy this picture. It may be valuable.
No it's good that you saved that. For women. And she told me.
She said, oh no. She said, well it's good to save it anyhow.
So we just kept it.
So from drawer to drawer that picture would travel and my kids and everything.
Yeah, lucky you saved that.
Yeah, I was interested in it, you know, that's why.
Are there any other favorite musicians you had? Who was the best trumpet players in the old days that you liked to hear or play with?
I used to like to hear Renee, I used to like to hear Celestan, Randy Perez during his time when he was living. And Euless Jean was good and Chris Kelly and Sam Morgan and Albert Snighy.
Yeah, I never heard him.
And my brother was a pretty good trumpet player. Yeah, he was a sweet waltz player. You couldn't find a man who played better trumpet than him. And he just takes six, taking six years.
Who were your favorite clarinet players? Anyone in particular that you can remember that you liked when you were young or you played with?
Well, I used to like to hear Willard Turner, Tuma at least.
What's the name again? Tuma, Will Tuma. Will.
Willard Tuma. And Adolf Alexander.
Oh yes. I knew him. Tats they called him.
And I played Tats. And I played with Louie Big Eye Louie.
Yeah.
I knew him. And I played with him quite a while.
Where did you work with him?
I worked with him in a little place but Dutchess on Frenchmen and Ferran.
Oh yes. That's before I got to hear him. Yeah. And I heard about the place.
Then I played with Pico for Dutchess on Cleveland and Frenchman. I played there about five years we played on that job.
Yeah I remember that place.

With Elmer Talbot. They used to have, Cuckoo used to play the clarinet. And the cornet and Albert Glennie was our bass player. That was his job. Harry Robichaux, Harry Robichaux used to be the ghetto player.
Yeah I heard him years ago.
And then my other favorite trumpet player was Schatz, Lewis Madison.
